How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iranians commute past a billboard depicting slain Lebanese Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran on September 27, 2026. ATTA KENARE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 16 October 2026 12 minutes How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” Three years of hostilities have transformed Tehran’s network of allies in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic is now relying more heavily on itself, while adapting its relationships with partners whose diminished military utility has not necessarily reduced its commitment to their protection. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Hamidreza Azizi Senior Analyst, Iran https://x.com/HamidRezaAz Related Tags Iran Israel/Palestine Lebanon Syria Developments since 7 October 2023, when Hamas staged its deadly attacks on southern Israel, have transformed Iran’s network of state and non-state allies in the Middle East, as well as their role in Tehran’s military planning and deterrence posture. The weakening of Hamas and Hizbollah at Israel’s hands in the last three years, the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria in December 2024 and, above all, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February have altered the vectors of Iranian influence. Together, these events have exposed the limits of an Iranian strategy that had relied chiefly on regional partners to deter adversaries and keep any armed confrontation away from Iran itself. Instead, Tehran now places greater weight on capabilities under its direct control: missiles, drones and the ability to obstruct traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. This evolution does not mean that the “ axis of resistance ”, as Iran calls its collection of allies, has lost all relevance. Rather, it means that axis members are now assuming different functions and that Tehran is approaching them differently. Yemen’s Houthis have gained particularly significant strategic value for Iran because their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping complements Tehran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. In Iraq, major Shiite factions also remain important political partners, even as Tehran increasingly turns to smaller armed groups to conduct military operations. Overall, the result is a more fragmented network in which heightened local autonomy among Iran’s non-state partners coexists with tighter Iranian control of select cells and smaller armed organisations. Nor is a weaker “axis of resistance” necessarily synonymous with diminished Iranian commitment to its partners. Hizbollah’s lesser contribution to Iranian deterrence, for example, has not reduced Tehran’s determination to protect the Lebanese Shiite movement. To the contrary, Iran has shown itself more willing to use force in Hizbollah’s defence; it also has conditioned reaching a deal terminating its hostilities with the United States on an end to Israel’s campaign in Lebanon. In other terms, Iran still may be drawn into conflicts on its regional partners’ behalf, even as they have become less capable of shielding it from attack. From the Levant to Maritime Chokepoints Prior to October 2023, Iran’s Middle East strategy centred on the Levant . Syria under Assad’s rule was the linchpin, the only Arab state allied with Iran, which provided it with substantial benefits: a land corridor linking Iran and its Iraqi Shiite partners to Hizbollah; proximity to Israel’s borders; and a logistical hub that enabled Tehran to project its influence to the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. In June 2024, Yahya Rahim Safavi , a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who was then military adviser to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, likened Iran’s reach through the axis to that of the ancient Persian empire under Cyrus and Xerxes. The advantages of alliance with Assad explain why, over a decade of civil war in Syria, Tehran defended his regime at significant cost. Hizbollah fighters also helped the regime a great deal, battling both its domestic opponents and ISIS. Hizbollah was useful in another important way, offering Tehran a means of threatening Israel from adjacent territory, thus ostensibly deterring it from direct strikes on Iran itself. If Assad’s Syria was a linchpin of the Islamic Republic’s Middle East strategy, the Shiite movement in Lebanon was a principal engine. [Assad’s fall] deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. This arrangement has suffered severe damage since October 2023 , when Hamas – apparently taking even Iran’s leadership by surprise – attacked Israel. The Gaza campaign that Israel launched in response dealt the axis a first blow, although Iran’s relationship with the Palestinian group has never been on par with those it has enjoyed with its other affiliates. Assad’s fall – indirectly part of the chain of events triggered by the Hamas attacks – was far more consequential. It deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. After Hizbollah entered the post-2023 fray, Israeli counter-attacks also inflicted substantial losses on the Lebanese movement’s leadership and military assets, while causing significant death, destruction and displacement in the country. As a result, other Lebanese factions began issuing more urgent calls on Hizbollah to disarm. The setbacks reinforced one another: rebuilding a degraded Hizbollah was a far more daunting task without the Syrian channel that had previously sustained it. These losses notwithstanding, Tehran has yet to forsake the Levant. Hizbollah still has a strong, institutionalised relationship with Iran, significant political weight in Lebanon and the capacity to regroup, at least in part. The Israeli incursions into southern Syria following the Assad regime’s demise may also have benefits for Iran. The Islamic Republic may be banking on local resistance to Israel eventually creating openings for renewed Iranian influence in Syria, though this prospect remains uncertain. For now, Iran has turned its attention to an arena closer to its borders where it retains heftier clout. On 8 June, Esmail Qaani , commander ofthe Revolutionary Guards’ overseas operations arm, the Qods Force, described an emerging “security belt” stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea. When compared to Safavi’s formulation two years prior, the phrase captures a shift in emphasis from the Levant to the maritime routes linking the Gulf to the western Indian Ocean, a theatre in which Iran’s sway comes more directly from its own place on the map. The Islamic Republic requires neither an allied state nor a non-state partner to project power in the Strait of Hormuz; it can station missiles and drones nearby or even deep inland to threaten naval or commercial vessels in these waters. Tehran’s influence over maritime routes upon which states near and far depend for trade in oil, gas and other vital commodities is boosted by its partnership with the Houthis, who can fire at ships passing in either direction through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Though it no longer serves as a land bridge for arms transfers to Syria and Lebanon, Iraq nonetheless plays an important part in this changing landscape. In particular, it is a locus for coordination between the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups , as well as between the Qods Force and Iraqi groups that have conducted attacks on Gulf Arab states. A More Fragmented Network The shift in Iran’s primary focus from the Levant to the seas has gone hand in hand with organisational changes. Under its late commander Qassem Soleimani, the Qods Force was the principal coordinator of “axis of resistance” activities. Since the U.S. killed Soleimani in January 2020, the Qods Force has not played the same role. Subsequent wars and leadership losses, both within the Revolutionary Guards and among its partners, further discombobulated command structures and impaired joint military operations. As a result, Iran has had to adapt its relationships with groups whose military capabilities and domestic constraints themselves have changed. It has increasingly been compelled to work through smaller groups or selected elements of established organisations. This trend has been most evident in Iraq. As the years passed after Saddam Hussein’s ouster, older Shiite political movements acquired key government positions and economic interests, thus becoming more beholden to popular constituencies. As a result, they are now more hesitant to engage in military action that risks provoking retaliation or eroding their standing. This reluctance was apparent early in the present U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, when several major Iraqi Shiite armed groups declined to mobilise on Tehran’s behalf. Iran had to rely on smaller, less prominent ones – drawn from the self-styled Islamic Resistance in Iraq – to come to its aid. Iraqi sources speak of a network of clandestine cells established by the Revolutionary Guards and operating outside established militias’ command structures that reportedly has been responsible for attacks on Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. These nimbler, smaller groups offer Tehran several advantages. They require fewer resources, they can conceal their affiliations and they can ignore the political constraints holding back their larger counterparts. Their greater ideological cohesion also arguably makes them easier for Tehran to direct. More institutionalised Iraqi Shiite groups remain important to Tehran, notwithstanding their reticence regarding military action in Iran’s defence. But their role has shifted: they are useful principally because they help Iran preserve influence in the country as well as the political space in which smaller armed groups are free to operate. Iran’s changing relationship with Hizbollah illustrates another type of adjustment to similar pressures. Though the movement retains a substantial organisation that helps Tehran sustain influence in Lebanon, Hizbollah’s military actions increasingly resemble those of a guerrilla group – quick-hitting raids that leave the group less vulnerable to Israeli airstrikes and intelligence penetration. Its use of first-person-view drones – drones using a live video feed from an onboard camera – to attack Israeli forces in southern Lebanon showcased the effectiveness of inexpensive technology, even as the movement has lost its more sophisticated capabilities. An Iranian expert with ties to both the Revolutionary Guards and Hizbollah told Crisis Group that Qods Force commanders have been directly involved in this revamping, including efforts to work through smaller units and help Hizbollah fighters adopt more agile tactics. Deterrence Moves Closer to Home, but the Axis Remains Important These changes reflect a broader reassessment of Iran’s deterrence posture. Its earlier approach heavily relied on the concept of “ forward defence ” ensured by regional partners, supplemented by the threat of direct retaliation from its own territory. The “axis of resistance” gave the Islamic Republic strategic depth , discouraging its adversaries from attacking it and keeping conflict distant from its borders. Only if that first layer of protection were to fail were Iranian missiles and drones to be used to shoot back. The past three years of war have starkly exposed the limits inherent in this arrangement. Iran’s regional network did not prevent direct attacks on the country – whether the major exchanges with Israel in 2024, the surprise Israeli attack in June 2025 or the more substantial confrontation with the U.S. and Israel beginning in February. As the deterrence value of axis partners dropped, Tehran was compelled to place greater weight on its own capabilities: missiles, drones and geographical leverage. If military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Yet, if military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Though the axis as a whole no longer serves as the primary foundation of Iran’s deterrence, decision-makers in Tehran believe that certain partners can play important roles in particular circumstances as they magnify Iran’s own capabilities and geographical leverage. Their experience during the present conflict with the U.S. has only bolstered this conviction. The Houthis have attained particular importance in the Islamic Republic’s thinking, which helps explain reports that Tehran has provided them with both guidance and military assistance. Tehran’s efforts in July to establish direct flights to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen illustrated the multidimensional nature of this support: the flights both challenged restrictions imposed by Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia on Houthi rule and reportedly carried Revolutionary Guards commanders, military advisers and missile- and drone-related equipment. Hizbollah, too, has retained its usefulness for Tehran. The movement attacked Israel following February’s U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, forcing Israel to contend with an additional front and placing further demands on its air defences. True, that supporting role was a far cry from the crucial deterrent function the movement was intended to play, a reflection of its diminished capabilities. Iranian officials have nevertheless continued to frame their confrontation with the U.S. and Israel as extending to Iran’s Middle East partners, Hizbollah in particular. In June, in a remarkable role reversal, Iran launched missiles at Israel in response to its campaign against Hizbollah, thereby marshalling its own forces in defence of its partner rather than the other way around. Moreover, it conditioned its acceptance of the (short-lived) 17 June memorandum of understanding halting hostilities with the U.S. on cessation of Israeli attacks in Lebanon: the opening clause explicitly included Lebanon in the ceasefire and affirmed Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel persisted with its offensive, however, including at Ali al-Taher , a strategic Hizbollah position in southern Lebanon where Israel besieged (and, in mid-September, demolished) an underground command and weapons complex. To Iranian officials, who had reportedly sent warnings that any such act would provoke a “forceful” response, the demolition was a reminder that Iranian threats of renewed missile attacks were an insufficient deterrent. Still, Iran’s stance showcased its commitment to axis members whose military utility has faded but not been erased. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. According to Iranian experts interviewed by Crisis Group, several members of the security establishment regard Hizbollah’s survival in particular as being closely tied to Iran’s own security, giving the relationship a significance that extends beyond the movement’s immediate military capabilities. This outlook has surfaced in public debates. In a January 2025 interview published by Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, former diplomat Hadi Seyyed Afghahi argued that pressure on militant groups in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen was aimed at “Iran and, more generally, the Shiites of the region”. Therefore, Tehran could not remain indifferent to these groups’ fate. Likewise, in December 2025, Ali Samadzadeh , an analyst with close ties to the regime, argued that Iran should be prepared to intervene militarily if Israel attacked Hizbollah, describing an assault on Lebanon as a prelude to renewed war with Iran. Defending regional partners, in this view, is part and parcel of protecting Iran itself. In short, where Tehran regards a partner as key to its own security, the fact that the partner has been weakened arguably – and perhaps paradoxically – provides Iran with added reason to intervene on its behalf. Efforts to curb Iranian influence by targeting allied groups may therefore draw Tehran into conflicts – a marked departure from the role these groups once played in shielding the Islamic Republic from direct involvement in hostilities. The extent of Iranian involvement is likely to depend on the particular relationship in question and the risks and costs inherent in intervention. But the bottom line is that its partners’ diminished military capabilities will not necessarily reduce Iran’s exposure to, or participation in, their respective conflicts. A Shifting Picture After three years of hostilities involving Iran’s partners and, since February, Iran itself, the “axis of resistance” is neither down nor out, but it is not what it once was, either in the function it serves or in Tehran’s relationship to its various members. The changes have been manifold. First, some of its members’ military capabilities have been significantly degraded. Secondly, direct confrontation with the U.S. and Israel has revealed the groups’ limited deterrent value and their inability to keep conflict away from Iranian territory. Finally, and partly as a result of their lessened status, they have come under growing domestic political, economic and security pressure, hindering their ability to directly participate in confrontations involving the Islamic Republic. These changes do not rule out these groups’ continued close operational ties to Tehran; nor do they mean an end to Iran’s commitment to their protection. But, together, they constrain the groups’ freedom of action. As a result, the focus of the Islamic Republic’s strategic doctrine has pivoted from allied non-state actors toward its own capabilities. This adjustment undoubtedly has preserved Iran’s ability to project power in its neighbourhood. But it does not come without serious risk, insofar as it has led Tehran to more directly bear the costs and dangers of confrontation. The Islamic Republic may well find ways to manage the consequences of its partners’ weakened clout by coming to their aid when they are endangered, giving them breathing space to regroup and using its own military assets to deter its foes, including by ensuring that others – notably Gulf Arab states – suffer the consequences of Middle East war. In so doing, Iran hopes to discourage future attacks. But this approach also risks deepening hostility among its neighbours, potentially encouraging closer security cooperation among Iran’s adversaries and heightening the very pressures Tehran seeks to reduce. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. The Dilemmas Facing Palestinian Citizens in Israel’s Elections mloukili Thu, 10/22/2026 - 16:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 22 October 2026 7 minutes The Dilemmas Facing Palestinian Citizens in Israel’s Elections Originally published in ISPI Arab-led parties could hold the balance of power in Israel's election. But as Palestinian citizens seek safety and equal rights, rival strategies and rejection by Jewish opposition leaders threaten to turn electoral leverage into political exclusion. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Amjad Iraqi Senior Analyst, Israel/Palestine https://x.com/aj_iraqi Related Tags Israel/Palestine In Arab towns and cities across Israel, streets and buildings are lined with posters and billboards about the upcoming national elections on 27 October. Two slates representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – a tri-party alliance called the Joint List (made up of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) and the United Arab List, also known as Ra’am – are competing for the community’s votes, which, according to polls, could give the parties a combined total of 13 to 15 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Many Palestinian citizens would agree that this election may be one of the most consequential in recent memory. But depending on who you ask, the principal contenders for their ballots appear either strikingly different or strangely similar. Despite an expanding matrix of laws and policies rendering them second-class citizens, Palestinians in Israel have long used their right to vote to assert their voice in the Knesset and to procure State resources to meet their socioeconomic needs. This year, fear has been a major driving motive . The far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has waged a relentless campaign against Palestinians – from the devastating war in Gaza, to heightened settler violence and accelerated annexation in the West Bank, to greater repression and discrimination inside Israel. Under the Ministry of National Security headed by Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s police have condoned, even more so than in the past, the organised crime and gun violence that have mushroomed in Arab localities, making personal security the top priority for most Arab voters. In theory, the Palestinian community – which makes up a fifth of Israel’s citizenry and about 17% of eligible voters – has some leverage to alter this state of affairs. Its clout derives not just from sheer numbers but from the fractured nature of Israel’s political landscape. Polls consistently show that neither Netanyahu’s ruling coalition nor the Jewish opposition led by Yashar! leader Gadi Eisenkot can secure a parliamentary majority on their own. Projections give the Joint List eight to nine seats and Ra’am five to six seats, with commentators describing the parties as potential “kingmakers” . Yet the projections tell only part of the story of a deeper schism at the heart of Palestinian politics in Israel and of the dilemmas that Arab voters face as they try to protect their rights – and indeed, their very presence – in the heart of an increasingly aggressive Israeli State. Unwanted Partners Given the likely shortfall in the Knesset, logic would dictate that the anti-Netanyahu bloc should partner with the Arab parties to oust the long-time prime minister and his far-right allies such as Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. Yet political prejudices are outweighing electoral mathematics . Almost all the Jewish opposition parties insist that they will not ally themselves with their Arab counterparts , with some even refusing to accept them as external backers of a minority government. Some, like Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, are open about their hostility towards Palestinian citizens, and some, like Together leader Naftali Bennett, worry about discouraging Jewish voters still reeling from Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks. Other still, such as Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid, are reluctant to be constrained by the demands of Arab parties. Eisenkot himself has said that he is seeking to build a “Zionist majority” coalition and that none of the Arab lists meets his criteria for partnership, such as supporting mandatory national service in the army or in civilian bodies (towards which Palestinian citizens are largely hostile), recognising Israel as a “Jewish and democratic” State (thereby accepting its ethno-nationalist character) and labelling Hamas a terrorist organisation. Split Responses Shunned and delegitimised as they are, the Joint List and Ra’am still insist they are prepared to play a part in deciding the next Israeli government. They have few illusions about an Eisenkot-led coalition, whose leaders echo many of Netanyahu’s right-wing views. Nonetheless, both Arab slates strongly believe that a renewed mandate for the far-right could amount to an existential threat to the community, let alone to Palestinians in the occupied territories. They argue that it is incumbent upon them to prevent Netanyahu’s return by any political means at their disposal. As one Arab parliamentarian put it to the International Crisis Group (ICG), “Our goal is to slow the bleeding – and I don’t mean that metaphorically”. While recognising the common danger, the two slates are at odds over how to wield their leverage . According to Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen , the tri-party alliance is ready to provide a “safety net” for an Israeli minority government as external backers in Parliament if the government pledges to tackle organised crime, halt punitive home demolitions and open a diplomatic pathway towards a Palestinian State. This offer has its antecedents: in the 1990s, Arab parties gave former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin external parliamentary support in the context of the Oslo Accords, and in 2019 and 2020, the Joint List offered its backing to Blue and White leader Benny Gantz to eject Netanyahu (which Gantz rejected). For Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas , though, any demands that relate to the occupation are likely to hinder cooperation with Jewish parties, which have grown more hawkish on the Palestinian question, at the expense of advancing the Arab community’s pressing needs. While in principle supportive of Palestinian rights and statehood, Ra’am has campaigned almost exclusively on the pledges of fighting crime and securing fresh budgets, even allying himself with former police commander and Jewish politician Yoav Segalovitz to signal that focus. Abbas, who made Ra’am a partner in the 2021-22 Bennett-Lapid government, argues that when it comes to decision making, “Either you are at the table, or you are left to the side”. Murky Prospects Experts generally agree that Palestinian citizens’ turnout at the ballot is likely to be high, with some estimating it could reach about 60-65% of eligible Arab voters. But many of those voters feel torn between two rival slates that may have little hope of acquiring the influence they claim is within their reach. If Eisenkot expects to be prime minister, he would have to either swallow his antagonism towards the Arab parties or partner with members of the rival bloc, perhaps even Netanyahu’s Likud. When faced with the same choice in 2020 after two inconclusive election rounds, Gantz opted to ally with Netanyahu. Though Eisenkot insists he will not do the same, it remains to be seen whether numerical necessity will press him toward a national unity government with Likud. Recent weeks have only deepened the murkiness. In September, with overwhelming endorsement from both coalition and opposition members, the Knesset’s Central Elections Committee disqualified the two Arab slates and two Arab politicians from running in the election. The Supreme Court overturned most of the decisions, but it supported the disqualification of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh over an article he had written describing the 7 October attacks as an “important historic event” and compelled him to either quit the race or receive a more consequential legal ruling; ultimately, he chose to bow out. Regardless of the court’s other rulings, the near-unanimous disdain towards the Arab parties delivered a chilling message that tolerance for Palestinians in the Knesset was wearing thin and that more political attacks on their representatives were likely in store. Internal disputes are also souring Arab voters. Some have been frustrated by the Joint List’s squabbles over how to allocate seats among its three parties, by a public saga over a now-ejected Hadash politician accused of sexual harassment and by disputes over the handling of Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification case. Meanwhile, some blame Ra’am for refusing to learn from the limitations it faced under the Bennett-Lapid government (such as when Ra’am members refused to join the coalition in passing a law that enshrined Israel’s ban on Palestinian family unification), for unduly taking credit for budgets secured by the Joint List in prior years, and for ignoring Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank at a time when they are being subjected to horrendous violence and suffering. Tensions Between Strategies With so much at stake, Palestinian citizens are desperate for a breakthrough in the coming elections. For some, Ra’am arguably offers the more pragmatic way forward. “The modern Arab voter is not interested in the old slogans” promoted by Arab parties, one political analyst told the International Crisis Group. Some Joint List supporters privately confess that Abbas is making a strong and coherent case for his approach. Several have even questioned the Joint List’s claim that its strategy is fundamentally different from Ra’am’s , further arguing that Ra’am’s focus on domestic issues could persuade the opposition to include it in a governing coalition and, in exchange for its support, agree to provide resources to address crime and violence – or at a minimum keep the far-right out of power. Still, Ra’am’s near-term pragmatism stands in tension with the Joint List’s long-term warning that Israel’s military rule over Palestinians beyond the Green Line cannot be detached from the shrinking rights of Palestinians inside the line. With Israel’s political spectrum sliding further rightwards, Arab parties have been among the only voices inside Israel reminding the country that the occupation is an existential problem . Ejecting the far-right could help reduce the speed and severity of Israel’s policies, but Netanyahu’s successors may prove to be almost as determined to preserve Israeli supremacy. As such, few Palestinian citizens believe that this election can bring about seismic changes. Their priorities are instead to mitigate Israel’s harms and restore some semblance of safety . The Arab parties are promising that they can advance these goals by clinching a large share of Knesset seats. Yet their voters will need other factors to make their voices count: a Jewish-Israeli politics that respects non-Jews as equals, a revitalised Palestinian leadership to guide the wider, broken national movement and a mix of international pressure and engagement to turn the conflict towards more constructive paths. REUTERS / Adnan Abidi Report 360 / Asia-Pacific 23 October 2026 20+ minutes A Trigger in Jammu and Kashmir: Militant Violence under Indian Central Rule In 2019, India made far-reaching changes to governance in Jammu and Kashmir, with the aim of quelling insurgency. Its policy has succeeded in some ways, but backfired in others. New Delhi will need to shift tack if it hopes to bring peace to the region. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags India Pakistan What’s new? Seven years after New Delhi revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status, ostensibly to curb militant activity and bring peace in its stead, disaffection is festering among Kashmiri Muslims. Militant groups are evolving in both their tactics and their chosen targets. Why does it matter? New Delhi’s tough security approach in the region has sparked a militant response. A deadly terrorist attack in April 2025 triggered clashes between India and Pakistan that ended in a stalemate. Another incident in Indian-administered Kashmir or elsewhere in India could once again trigger conflict between the two nuclear powers. What should be done? New Delhi should push forward plans to restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, hand powers back to regional authorities and rein in its harsh, counterproductive use of anti-terror laws. India and Pakistan, with the support of foreign governments, should seek to revive high-level back channels to prevent a future confrontation. Executive Summary Seven years after India revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s semi-autonomous status and ushered in sweeping reforms, ostensibly to bring peace to the Himalayan region, bitterness festers. Despite improvements in security, the changes that New Delhi foisted on the population are fuelling resentment of the Indian state while failing to uproot militant groups, which have gone underground. The repercussions go far beyond Indian-administered Kashmir. A massacre of tourists in April 2025 in the region triggered a four-day conflict between India and Pakistan after New Delhi blamed Islamabad. A ceasefire is now in place, but another terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir or elsewhere in India could unleash fresh interstate fighting. Given these risks, New Delhi should reconsider its heavy-handed approach to governance in Jammu and Kashmir. It should also restore statehood to the region, with the aim of strengthening local rule and depriving insurgents of their main rallying cry. Friendly countries should support détente between India and Pakistan, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse the potential for conflict. After proclaiming changes to Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional status in August 2019, the Indian government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), moved aggressively to pre-empt unrest, locking down public spaces, placing restrictions on communications and religious practices, and arresting politicians and activists from across the spectrum. These measures stymied opposition to New Delhi’s takeover, but they also disrupted traditional channels of political dialogue between Kashmiris and the Indian state. With protests banned and both separatist and pro-India politicians either jailed or under house arrest, channels for airing grievances were sealed shut. New Delhi ... sought to reshape Kashmiri politics by supporting new parties, sidelining established ones and redesigning constituencies to influence electoral results. New Delhi also sought to reshape Kashmiri politics by supporting new parties, sidelining established ones and redesigning constituencies to influence electoral results. Before holding regional polls in September 2024, the central government curtailed the powers of the chief minister, the highest political officeholder in the region, by shifting responsibilities to a lieutenant governor named by New Delhi. When the polls took place, Kashmiris chose to vent their fury at the central government’s policies by opposing the BJP. But with the new regional government rendered largely toothless, public discontent has not abated. Amendments to Jammu and Kashmir’s domicile and land laws, meanwhile, have aggravated locals’ feelings of impotence. The BJP government says these changes will boost economic growth, but Kashmiris are worried that New Delhi is plotting to redraw the region’s demographics by allowing non-Kashmiris to settle in India’s only Muslim-majority region. With limited political representation to count on, these concerns have been ignored by policymakers in the capital. Indian officials seem convinced they will be able to maintain control of the region through a combination of fear, force and the promise of development. But Kashmiri Muslims perceive the government’s decisions to be driven by religious discrimination, describing its approach as “collective punishment”. Though most Kashmiris abhor the killing of civilians, Crisis Group research since 2021 suggests that tacit support for militants who resort to such violence is on the rise in some quarters. While the government’s campaign has thinned their ranks, these groups are still able to carry out large-scale attacks at opportune moments. Militants, for their part, are intent on winning wider public support. New outfits with secular names such as The Resistance Front and the United Liberation Front of Kashmir have emerged, though authorities say they are merely rebranded anti-India jihadist groups operating from Pakistan, allegations that Islamabad denies. These outfits go to great lengths to conceal their activities. As India’s forces focus on the Muslim-majority Kashmir valley, militants have also increasingly turned their sights on Hindu-majority Jammu, catching authorities off guard. Tactics have changed as well. At the heart of the militants’ campaign is opposition to efforts to remake the region’s social and religious identity. A series of killings of non-local civilians by these groups, including the April 2025 massacre in Pahalgam in which 26 mostly Hindu tourists were killed, seems designed to exploit antipathy for government policies, particularly the change in legislation allowing non-Kashmiris to settle in the region. A suicide bombing that killed fifteen in November 2025 in New Delhi has likewise inflamed concerns about an uptick in jihadist violence. New Delhi’s uncompromising measures have fuelled anger in Kashmir while seemingly failing to eradicate [militant] groups. In the Indian government’s opinion, the militants’ selection of soft targets suggests that the insurgency is fading away. But New Delhi’s uncompromising measures have fuelled anger in Kashmir while seemingly failing to eradicate these groups. Accusations that Pakistan is supporting Kashmiri militants have also ratcheted up tensions with Islamabad, which rejects the allegations and attributes Kashmiri discontent to India’s heavy-handed policies in the region. Following the Pahalgam attack, New Delhi conducted airstrikes on alleged “terrorist infrastructure” in Pakistan, triggering a four-day conflict between the two nuclear-armed states that caused worldwide alarm. The display of Pakistan’s fighting capabilities during these short-lived clashes appears to have bolstered support for Islamabad among some Kashmiri Muslims, who look to Pakistan as a bulwark of resistance to New Delhi. Indeed, many locals believe Pakistan has ramped up its backing for militant groups, though they provide no conclusive evidence to that effect. New Delhi should shift tack if it wishes to bring lasting peace to the region. It should restore statehood to Jammu and Kashmir, as a first step toward reducing public distrust of the Indian state, and return powers to the chief minister in recognition of the region’s demand for greater autonomy. Indian officials should also roll back the clampdown, particularly the use of harsh anti-terror laws against anyone even suspected of militant ties. The high risk of renewed conflict between India and Pakistan also underscores the importance of resuming bilateral dialogue. Given the limited appetite in New Delhi for such engagement, quiet diplomacy through a high-level back channel remains the best option. Foreign governments with influence in both New Delhi and Islamabad should discreetly encourage the two governments to rekindle contacts that can foster mutual trust and lower the danger of a wider conflagration. After close to four decades of conflict, achieving durable peace in Indian-administered Kashmir and preventing a resumption of war with Pakistan will require bold moves that look beyond counter-insurgency and central government diktat. New Delhi/Srinagar/Brussels, 23 October 2026 Poonch district in Jammu lies on the border with Pakistan. With the security campaign focused in Kashmir, militants expanded their focus south across the Pir Panjal range to Jammu. Poonch, Jammu, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi I. Introduction For decades, Jammu and Kashmir has been a hive of separatist militancy in India and a source of friction in the country’s relations with neighbouring Pakistan. What is now Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir was once part of a princely state that was hotly disputed between India and Pakistan upon partition in 1947. For the next two years, the two countries went to war over the territory, which was split in two by a ceasefire, with both sides since claiming it in its entirety. They have clashed several times since then. In 1951, India granted semi-autonomous status to the portion of the Himalayan region it controls. This area is itself divided by topography and majority religion. Jammu, lying closer to the rest of India south of the Pir Panjal mountain range, is mostly Hindu. Muslim-majority Kashmir is nestled in a valley between the Pir Panjals and the towering Himalayas to the north and east. In 2019, the Indian government made far-reaching changes to the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir. Officials claimed that these reforms would put an end to the insurgency that had been raging against Indian rule since 1989, calling either for merging the territory with Pakistan or declaring it an independent country. In many ways, New Delhi’s intervention appears to have been successful: the frequency of militant attacks has declined, as has the number of active militants, and violent street protests have almost vanished. But in other respects, not least that popular resentment of the Indian state has intensified, the 2019 measures appear to have backfired. This report takes the political temperature in Indian-administered Kashmir seven years after New Delhi took away the region’s semi-autonomous status. It looks at the policies New Delhi has pursued in the interim and the new sorts of militancy that are emerging, despite the state’s clampdown, as a result. It then assesses the chances of further confrontations between India and Pakistan related to Kashmir, before suggesting some ways of dialling down tensions both inside and surrounding the region. The report is based on field research in both the Kashmir valley and the Jammu area, including roughly 60 interviews with state officials, Kashmiri politicians and ordinary Kashmiris. About a tenth of the interviewees were women, reflecting their low representation in the region’s public sphere. The report also draws upon Crisis Group’s past publications on the Kashmir dispute. 1 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°185, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , 17 September 2025; Crisis Group Statement, “ Pulling India and Pakistan Back from the Brink ”, 8 May 2025; Crisis Group Commentary, “ Keeping Kashmir on the Radar ”, 27 January 2022; Crisis Group Asia Report N°310, Raising the Stakes in Jammu and Kashmir , 5 August 2020; Crisis Group Commentary, “ Calming India and Pakistan’s Tit-for-Tat Escalation ”, 1 March 2019; Crisis Group Commentary, “ Deadly Kashmir Suicide Bombing Ratchets Up India-Pakistan Tensions ”, 22 February 2019; Crisis Group Asia Report N°224, Pakistan’s Relations with India: Beyond Kashmir? , 3 May 2012; Crisis Group Asia Report N°79, India/Pakistan Relations and Kashmir: Steps Toward Peace , 24 June 2004; Crisis Group Asia Report N°69, Kashmir: The View From New Delhi , 4 December 2003; Crisis Group Asia Report N°68, Kashmir: The View From Islamabad , 4 December 2003; Crisis Group Asia Report N°70, Kashmir: Learning from the Past , 4 December 2003; Crisis Group Asia Report N°41, Kashmir: The View From Srinagar , 21 November 2002; Crisis Group Asia Report N°35, Kashmir: Confrontation and Miscalculation , 11 July 2002. II. The Centre Takes Hold A. A Hostile Takeover On 5 August 2019, the Indian government declared that it was revoking what was commonly referred to as Article 370 – the clause in the Indian constitution that had granted semi-autonomy to the state of Jammu and Kashmir – and dividing the state into two union territories, both to be run by the central government. 2 The two union territories in question are Jammu and Kashmir, which is largely Muslim and was once a princely state, and sparsely populated Ladakh, which has a mix of Buddhists and Muslims. The central government had already dissolved the elected regional assembly in 2018, after the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) withdrew its support for the Jammu and Kashmir People’s Democratic Party, leaving it unable to muster a majority. It is likely that the BJP made this decision with an eye to minimising resistance to the forthcoming changes. For weeks prior to the announcement, the region had been on a knife’s edge. Kashmiris were rattled by several unexplained government decisions, such as asking tourists to leave the state (citing a supposed terrorist threat) and sending in an additional 40,000 troops. 3 Anuradha Bhasin, A Dismantled State: The Untold Story of Kashmir after Article 370 (Gurugram, 2023), p. 1. The valley was parcelled into small blocks, cordoned off on all sides and placed under lockdown. On 4 August, New Delhi imposed a communications blackout, cutting off the region from the rest of the world. Only the next day was it apparent that the government had taken these steps in anticipation of violent backlash to its measure revoking semi-autonomy. A local journalist described the 5 August announcement as “the biggest existential crisis” ever for Kashmiris under Indian rule, but the popular response was restrained. 4 Crisis Group interview, leading journalist, Srinagar, October 2021. Protests were certainly discouraged by the massive deployment of state forces. More important, however, was the absence of political figures who might have led the charge. As a precautionary measure, the central government had detained the entire Kashmiri political class, from pro-India mainstream politicians to separatist leaders who had boycotted electoral politics and, sometimes, embraced similar goals to the militants. 5 Most of the separatist leaders remain in jail to this day. “5161 persons taken into preventive custody in Kashmir valley since 4th August 2019: Shri. G. Kishan Reddy”, press release, Indian Ministry of Home Affairs, 4 December 2019. The harsh treatment meted out to mainstream politicians, many of whom had worked closely with central governments in the past, shocked Kashmiris, who saw it as evidence that New Delhi would never trust them, no matter how much loyalty they displayed. 6 “Ground report: Kashmir in shock and anger”, The Caravan , 16 August 2019. Three of the erstwhile state’s former chief ministers were among those detained. In hindsight, it is clear that the detentions weakened politicians who defended integration into India as the best choice for Kashmiris, as opposed to independence or joining Pakistan. 7 Prior to 2019, pro-India parties participated in elections and ran the regional government, whereas separatist forces rejected compliance with the Indian constitution. The government’s sweep did not stop at politicians, but reached into civil society as well, with figures such as journalists and human rights activists rounded up for alleged participation in separatist networks. In July 2019, before the proclamation of central rule, the National Investigation Agency, India’s top counter-terrorism and investigative body, summoned the editors of Greater Kashmir and The Kashmir Reader , two leading newspapers in the region, to question them about their sources of funding – a move that other local media outlets took as a warning. 8 Kunal Majumder, “Kashmir’s news media faces existential crisis amid restrictions, arrests”, Committee to Protect Journalists, 24 September 2019. Later, dozens of journalists were detained and investigated under severe anti-terror laws. 9 Bhasin, A Dismantled State , op. cit., pp. 161-166. The Kashmir Press Club in Srinagar was converted into a police station. By January 2020, the administration had introduced formal new restrictions on press freedom, including the threat of punishment for publishing material the authorities deemed “unethical” or “anti-national”. 10 Auqib Javed, “Kashmir’s new media policy menaces its media”, Article 14, 6 July 2020. For many Kashmiris, the fact that the clampdown was the work of a government led by the ... BJP gave it an unmistakable hue of religious discrimination. By such means, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government showed that it meant business in establishing control of India’s sole Muslim-majority region. Its approach marked a departure from previous practice, which had typically involved a combination of sleight of hand and coercion in managing conflict. For many Kashmiris, the fact that the clampdown was the work of a government led by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) gave it an unmistakable hue of religious discrimination. The closure of the Grand Mosque in Srinagar and the months-long detention of its chief cleric – Kashmir’s most prominent religious figure, known by the title Mirwaiz – deepened this impression. 11 “In Kashmir, closed mosque belies India’s religious freedom”, AP, 16 December 2021. Kashmiris were quick to dub the government’s moves “collective punishment”, saying they now lived in an “open-air prison”. 12 “Kashmir turned into an open-air prison”, Jacobin , 9 December 2019. Across the rest of India, on the other hand, public opinion proved overwhelmingly supportive of the changes imposed by New Delhi. Most Indians bought the government’s argument that its reforms were an antidote to separatism and would spur an economic boom in Kashmir. Fresh from a second successive landslide in the April-May 2019 national elections, the BJP was riding a nationalist wave. During the campaign, it had capitalised on anger about a suicide attack that had killed over 40 security personnel in Pulwama, Indian-administered Kashmir, in February 2019. 13 Crisis Group Commentary, “ Deadly Kashmir Suicide Bombing Ratchets Up India-Pakistan Tensions ”, op. cit. The BJP portrayed itself as the party that would avenge these deaths and Modi as the country’s “guardian”. 14 The BJP used the Hindi term chowkidar , which means “guard” or “watchman”. “Pakistan, terrorism, chowkidar – Modi’s favourite words in speeches after Pulwama attack”, The Print , 11 April 2019. The Pulwama attack reportedly firmed up the government’s resolve to repeal Article 370, a pledge the BJP had included in its manifesto since 1983. Rahul Pandita, The Lover Boy of Bahawalpur: How the Pulwama Case Was Cracked (New Delhi, 2021), p. 140. Much of the national media also amplified New Delhi’s contention that Kashmiris were celebrating the changes imposed upon them . 15 “ Republic World : ‘Modi corrects Nehru’s Kashmir blunder’”, video, YouTube, 6 August 2019. B. Behind the Iron Curtain Following the government’s decision to cut off internet and mobile connectivity, Kashmir became an information black hole, making it impossible to keep tabs on events as they unfolded. 16 “Kashmir group calls India’s internet ban ‘digital apartheid’”, AP, 25 August 2020. The Indian home minister was probably correct when he said Kashmir had been “integrated” without a single bullet being fired or a single person dying. 17 “Kashmir integrated without a single bullet: Amit Shah”, The Times of India , 27 October 2019. But the repression was nonetheless intense. According to the few media reports that exist, state forces went after young people from southern Kashmir, which is known for being a hotbed of separatism, beating them with sticks and rods as well as using other forms of torture, including hanging them upside down for prolonged periods and applying electric shocks, to prevent disturbances. 18 See, for example, “With meticulous planning, then mass arrests, and ‘torture’, Kashmir’s autonomy was lost”, The Independent , 1 September 2019; “The night the soldiers came: Allegations of abuse surface in Kashmir”, The Washington Post , 30 September 2019; “‘Don’t beat us, just shoot us’: Kashmiris allege violent crackdown”, BBC, 30 August 2019. Fact-finding reports by civil society organisations also noted cases of sexual harassment of Kashmiri women during search operations conducted at night. 19 Crisis Group interview, woman student from Pulwama district, Srinagar, November 2025. Due to social stigma among the Muslims of Kashmir, violence against women often goes unreported. See Bhasin, A Dismantled State , op. cit., pp. 76-77; and “Annual Human Rights Review 2019”, Jammu and Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society, December 2019. Seven years later, many such incidents have not yet come to light. A senior journalist quoted the Kashmiri poet Agha Shahid Ali (himself echoing Tacitus) when reflecting on New Delhi’s assertion of control: “They make a desolation and call it peace”. 20 Crisis Group interview, leading journalist, Srinagar, August 2023. Soon after imposing a national lockdown in March 2020 following the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Indian government pushed through further changes. A week into the lockdown, New Delhi amended Jammu and Kashmir’s domicile law, making Indians from other parts of the country eligible for permanent residency in the territory, as well as for public-sector jobs. 21 The government enabled itself repealing Article 35A of the constitution – which defined who was a permanent resident of Jammu and Kashmir and their rights, and restricted non-residents from holding government jobs or owning land within the state – along with Article 370. The move unnerved Kashmiris, who perceived it as the first step in a campaign to alter the region’s demographics to the detriment of local Muslims. 22 Crisis Group interviews, locals including journalists, officials and political leaders, Kashmir, 2019-2025. In October, New Delhi announced new laws allowing non-residents to purchase land in the region, even though Jammu and Kashmir, along with a few other states, had long enjoyed special protections to safeguard its culture. 23 “Ominously anti-federal: On the Supreme Court’s judgment on Article 370 and J&K’s special status”, The Hindu , 12 December 2023; “What is Article 371 and what are the protections it provides?”, The Hindu , 9 May 2024. With no elected representatives to appeal to or channels for conveying their discontent, Kashmiris grew increasingly convinced that the government was intent on bringing in non-Kashmiris to convert them into a minority. 24 “India’s residency law in Kashmir amplifies demographic fears”, AP, 5 August 2020. Under house arrest, Kashmir’s pre-eminent separatist leader, Syed Ali Geelani, who had long warned of such a risk, urged people to resist the reforms. 25 “Hurriyat leader Syed Ali Shah Geelani asks Kashmiris to resist, issues ‘program of action’”, Scroll.in , 25 August 2019. “J&K: Geelani sees plot to change Muslim majority”, The New Indian Express , 16 May 2012. The government then started to redraw electoral constituencies in Jammu and Kashmir. It justified the move as part of the reorganisation initiated in 2019, but locals perceived it as gerrymandering intended to benefit the BJP – which, as a Hindu nationalist party, is more influential in the Hindu-majority Jammu region than in the Muslim-majority Kashmir valley – and yet another measure designed to deprive them of a political voice. 26 Praveen Donthi, “ Flare-Ups and Frustration as Kashmir Waits for a Vote ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 8 March 2024. The delimitation commission appointed by the government eventually added six new constituencies to the Jammu division and only one to the Kashmir division, which has a larger population but is 97 per cent Muslim, leading to accusations that the commission was acting in the BJP’s service. 27 Ibid. The population of Jammu stands at 5.3 million, whereas that of the Kashmir valley is 6.8 million. Those charged with delimitation should normally redraw electoral constituencies according to population size, to ensure that each elected representatives correspond has roughly an equal number of constituents. In combination, the closure of avenues of political representation, the crackdown on dissent and the battery of other reforms heightened Kashmiris’ anxiety about the future. For some of them, these developments also gave rise to a newfound sympathy for militant groups. 28 In the only Srinagar neighbourhood to witness protests in August 2019, demonstrators chanted the slogan, “One solution, gun solution”. See “Ground report: Kashmir in shock and anger”, op. cit. It may have been a sign of things to come. C. Seeking International Attention Kashmiris hoped that Pakistan – and its close ally China – would intervene in international forums to draw attention to the region’s plight. Both countries did indeed raise concerns about India’s actions at the UN. Asserting that any change in Jammu and Kashmir’s disputed status violated UN resolutions, Islamabad downgraded its diplomatic relations with New Delhi and expelled the Indian high commissioner; India responded in kind. Imran Khan, Pakistan’s prime minister, penned an op-ed in The New York Times , warning that if the world did not “stop the Indian assault on Kashmir” it would face “consequences … as two nuclear-armed states get ever closer to a direct military confrontation”. 29 Imran Khan, “The world can’t ignore Kashmir: We are all in danger”, The New York Times , 30 August 2019. Beijing also sharply criticised New Delhi, telling the UN Security Council that India had “challenged China’s sovereign interests” and was stoking regional tensions. 30 China holds an area called Aksai Chin, which was part of Jammu and Kashmir when it was a princely state. Beijing seized these lands in the 1962 Sino-Indian war; New Delhi claims them as part of Ladakh. “UNSC Kashmir moot gives lie to Indian claim”, Dawn , 17 August 2019; “Chinese Stance in United Nations Security Council towards India”, Vivekananda International Foundation, 15 October 2020. Despite these condemnations, many Kashmiris were disappointed that Islamabad failed to mobilise meaningful international pressure on India to reverse its actions. 31 Crisis Group interviews, Kashmiri residents, Srinagar, November 2023. Their sense of abandonment only deepened when Prime Minister Modi, visiting Washington in September 2019, announced that India was building a “new Kashmir”, getting no pushback from U.S. officials. 32 Crisis Group interviews, journalists, academics and politicians, Srinagar, 2021. “We will build a ‘new’ Kashmir for everyone says PM Modi to Kashmiri pandits in Houston”, The Hindu , 22 September 2019. New Delhi’s post-2019 security crackdown in Jammu and Kashmir suppressed militancy, but militants remain capable of conducting big attacks like in Pahalgam of April 2025. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi III. Politics and Militants in the “New Kashmir” As India’s central government tightened its grip on Kashmir, fear grew among locals that New Delhi was intent on transforming the Muslim-majority region. With little support for its cause among Kashmiris, New Delhi opted to continue ruling the region through its appointed representative. Meanwhile, its stranglehold on Kashmir forced militants to change their tactics, posing new challenges to Indian authorities. A. Re-engineering the Political Landscape After altering the status of Jammu and Kashmir, the federal government sought to bring about a new political configuration in the region, one that New Delhi would find “absolutely pliable”, as a Kashmiri journalist put it. 33 Crisis Group interview, leading Kashmiri journalist, Srinagar, 2023. While prominent local leaders remained under arrest and political activity was curtailed, new parties favoured by the central government endeavoured to win public support. They failed to do so, however, as the vast majority of Kashmiris perceived them as BJP proxies. 34 Bhasin, A Dismantled State , op. cit., p. 188. Alongside its support for new parties, the Indian government sought to redraw electoral constituencies for regional and national elections (see Section II.B). 35 “Jammu and Kashmir: The hidden agenda behind the delimitation exercise”, Frontline , 2 April 2022. The BJP hoped that the extra seats it created in Jammu would help it secure a majority in the regional assembly once new elections were called, enabling it to establish an administration that would not depend on coalitions with Kashmiri parties. New Delhi nevertheless appeared uncertain that the new formula would deliver. It remained reluctant to hold regional elections until the Supreme Court ordered it to do so by September 2024. 36 Ibid. The first major polls held in Jammu and Kashmir after the 2019 changes were the national parliamentary elections, which took place in June 2024. Aware of popular anger at the central government, the BJP did not contest the region’s three national constituencies. One of the region’s two largest parties and its oldest, the Jammu and Kashmir National Conference, won two, while Kashmiris sent an emphatic message to Indian authorities in the third by electing an independent, Sheikh Abdul Rashid, a 58-year-old politician who had been in jail since August 2019 on charges of “terror funding” and receiving funds from Pakistan. 37 Rashid remains in prison, but the court allows him to attend parliamentary proceedings in police custody. “‘Vote against jail’: How two Modi critics won India election from prison”, Al Jazeera, 14 June 2024; “Kashmir: Why Modi’s BJP is not fighting elections in the Himalayan region”, BBC, 11 May 2024. Defiant, he called his win “a referendum against all sorts of oppression” and said the calm in Kashmir should not be interpreted as “real peace”. 38 “Engineer Rashid delivers victory message with a sting”, The Telegraph , 12 June 2024. Voter discontent was ... plain to see in the regional polls in September, which saw a high turnout of 63 per cent. Voter discontent was also plain to see in the regional polls in September, which saw a high turnout of 63 per cent. Though they had previously called on Kashmiris to boycott elections, separatist politicians backed the vote on this occasion, arguing that citizens needed an administration run by locals, which could provide a measure of relief from constant repression, rather than bureaucrats who had parachuted in. 39 Praveen Donthi, “ Kashmir Votes to Repudiate Rule from the Centre ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 October 2024. Voter participation in elections held in Jammu and Kashmir has historically been scant – as low as 3 per cent in one constituency in 2002 – due to factors ranging from separatism to fear of militant attack. Turnout was exceptionally high in the two most recent votes: 58 per cent for the national elections in April-May 2024 and 63 per cent during that October’s regional elections. “Jammu and Kashmir polls: Ups and downs in voter turnout”, The Hindu , 8 October 2024. The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference won 42 of 90 seats, becoming the largest political force in the new regional assembly; the party’s leader, Omar Abdullah, was elected chief minister – a position he had already held more than a decade ago. The BJP finished second with 29 seats, all of them in Hindu-majority Jammu, not Kashmir. “People responded to an undemocratic decision through democratic means, by registering their dissent”, a Kashmiri member of the federal parliament observed. 40 Crisis Group interview, Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, member of parliament, Budgam, 28 November 2025. Even so, the authority of the new regional assembly and the chief minister had been curbed well before the polls were held. The 2019 reforms had already diluted regional powers by turning the state into a union territory. Security and law enforcement, particularly land laws, fell under the purview of a lieutenant governor appointed by New Delhi. Between 2019 and the 2024 elections, New Delhi extended the lieutenant governor’s remit to include a final say on most legislative and administrative matters. By allowing normal political activity to resume, the vote opened space for public debate. But Kashmiris remain deeply dissatisfied with a setup they see as entrenching rule by outsiders. 41 Crisis Group interviews, journalists, politicians and academics, Srinagar, 2021-2025. Furthermore, the elected chief minister has few prerogatives, particularly as regards security. “Having two power centres anywhere is a recipe for disaster”, Chief Minister Abdullah himself commented. 42 “‘Recipe for disaster’: CM Omar Abdullah on dual governance model in J&K”, The Times of India , 14 December 2024. Having served in the post once before, he is well placed to understand the difference: when Jammu and Kashmir was a state, his office served as head of the unified command, integrating all the state’s security forces. Now, not only does he have no say in security matters, but he also lacks input into minor decisions such as appointing civil servants. 43 “‘Families devastated, review each case’: From Mehbooba to Omar, a letter on termination of 74 employees without hearing”, The Indian Express , 11 November 2024; “Raj Bhawan’s actions undermine elected government in J&K: Omar Abdullah”, The Hindu , 29 November 2025. B. A Chokehold on Militancy New Delhi’s post-2019 crackdown in Jammu and Kashmir suppressed militancy, but it did not put an end to this activity. State forces invoked two stringent anti-terror laws – the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act – which allow for holding detainees for up to six months without formal charges or trial. 44 “The UAPA and PSA are being used as tools of coercion in Kashmir”, Frontline , 23 March 2021. Beyond dismantling what it called the “terror ecosystem”, the government’s objective was also to “increase the social costs for supporting or becoming a militant”. 45 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Srinagar, 2025. The state started prosecuting anyone remotely linked to militants or their alleged associates, rather than just their immediate family and friends, as had long been the case. 46 Ibid. According to official data, 3,662 people have been arrested under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act between 2019 and 2023. No official data is available regarding arrests made under the Public Safety Act; however, according to media reports, at least 4,000 people were detained under this law in August 2019, and most recently the chief minister claimed that 400 people were in prison under it. See “J&K accounts for 35% of all UAPA arrests in India from 2019-2023, data reveals”, The New Indian Express , 4 December 2025; “At least 4,000 detained in Kashmir since region stripped of autonomy”, AFP, 18 August 2019; and “J&K CM Omar flags misuse of Public Safety Act against youth with no cases, claims 400 such arrests”, The Hindu , 7 March 2025. Firmly under New Delhi’s control, the regional authorities even dismissed public employees for security reasons, without due process. 47 See tweet by Omar Abdullah, @OmarAbdullah, former chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir, 8:22pm, 8 June 2024. The government took several other measures to quash militancy. For instance, state forces stopped returning slain militants’ bodies to their families, citing pandemic rules. The real reason, however, was that funerals had become occasions to lionise militants and inspire disgruntled young people to join the fight. 48 Not handing over dead bodies offended the religious sensibilities of Kashmiri people. “Kashmir: Why is anger rising over militant burials?”, Deutsche Welle, 30 November 2021. Soldiers also systematically demolished the houses of suspected militants’ families, as well as those of individuals suspected of aiding the insurgency in any way. 49 Bhasin, A Dismantled State , p. 121. These punitive measures served to stoke antipathy toward the Indian state. 50 “Youth share tales of harassment at PDP meet on why Kashmiri professionals are turning to violence”, The Hindu , 8 December 2025. In response, insurgents modified their tactics. Soon after August 2019, novel outfits with secular names such as The Resistance Front, the Kashmir Tigers, the People’s Anti-Fascist Front and the United Liberation Front of Kashmir emerged, emphasising opposition to the government’s efforts to alter the region’s socio-religious identity rather than the traditional separatist themes. 51 Crisis Group Report, Raising the Stakes in Jammu and Kashmir, op. cit. The message was designed to resonate with Kashmiris fearful that New Delhi was engineering demographic change. Many Kashmiris condemned [the militants' killings of "outsiders"], while continuing to oppose New Delhi’s legislative changes. A series of attacks mirrored the switch in rhetoric. From October 2019, militants killed a number of non-locals in the south of Indian-administered Kashmir, gunning down fruit traders and truck drivers, as well as migrant labourers – most of them Hindus, though the victims also included non-Kashmiri Muslims. 52 The number of militant attacks on state forces continued but declined slightly after 2019. Attacks on non-local civilians and local police officers increased, however. For instance, between 2014 and 2019, militants killed 170 civilians and 406 security personnel, but between August 2019 and November 2021 they killed 87 civilians and 99 security personnel. The gap between the number of civilian and security personnel deaths narrowed most in 2021 and 2022: 41 civilians and 42 security personnel were killed in 2021, and 31 and 32, respectively, in 2022. This trend continued from 2023 to 2025, when 73 civilians and 72 security personnel were killed. See “87 civilians, 99 security personnel killed in J&K since Article 370 scrapped: Govt”, The Hindu , 6 April 2022; “Security situation in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh”, press release, Indian Ministry of Home Affairs, 7 February 2024. Militants also began to deliberately attack the few Kashmiri Hindus who had not fled during the mass exodus in 1990 or had come back later. 53 The vast majority of Kashmiri pandits, as members of Jammu and Kashmir’s Hindu community are known, fled the region in the early 1990s due to militant threats. See Praveen Donthi, “ Violence in Kashmir: Why a Spike in Killings Signals Ominous New Trend ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 28 June 2022. While not all these victims would have been eligible for residency or jobs under Jammu and Kashmir’s new domicile laws introduced in 2020, the systematic targeting of “outsiders” sent an intimidating message to non-locals. Many Kashmiris condemned these killings, while continuing to oppose New Delhi’s legislative changes. Another trend that briefly emerged after 2019 was a series of assaults on Kashmiri police officers. 54 Crisis Group interview, mid-level security official, Srinagar, 2023. See also Donthi, “ Flare-Ups and Frustration as Kashmir Waits for a Vote ”, op. cit. Separatist leaders, who wielded influence over militants, had previously discouraged attacks on police on the grounds that, unlike Indian army soldiers, they are mostly locals; they feared that such incidents could spark intra-communal conflict. But with all the separatist leaders jailed in the aftermath of New Delhi’s intervention, the safeguard disappeared. A police officer told Crisis Group that the force used to be able to press separatist leaders into convincing militants not to attack its personnel. But the sudden changes in circumstances have meant the police are “playing a game without a referee”, demoralising the rank and file. 55 Ibid. New Delhi painted the militants’ choice of soft targets such as non-locals and police officers as a sign of weakness, asserting that a lack of weaponry, training and numbers had dissuaded them from attacking Indian security forces. Though this claim may have an element of truth, the full picture is more complex. One security official told Crisis Group that the militants’ aim in harming civilians was to trigger a disproportionate state response, in the belief that mass arrests would foster further disaffection with Indian authorities and support for insurgent groups. 56 Crisis Group interview, security official, Srinagar, 2023. Others believe the attacks may have been a cheap and easy means of discrediting the government’s narrative about achieving peace in Kashmir, as they made national and international headlines. 57 Crisis Group interviews, senior security officials, Jammu and Kashmir, 2023. The militants killed five non-local labourers on the day a delegation of EU parliamentarians visited Kashmir in October 2019, likely as a way of drawing international attention. See “Outrage over right-wing Euro MPs’ Kashmir visit”, BBC, 31 October 2019. The central government said its iron-fist approach of “comprehensively defeating” separatism was working, however, in part because it had countered the “substantial influence of Pakistan” on both Kashmiri public opinion and militant groups. 58 “The Straight Line: Pak control, narrative war, white-collar terror: Ex DGP of J&K R. S. Swain’s first big interview”, video, YouTube, 20 January 2026. Given the long history in Kashmir of protests spiralling out of control, the official priority was to “ensure the streets remain calm”. 59 Ibid. With the stone throwing, Kashmiri youth were modelling themselves on Palestinians during the two intifadas. In that regard, the crackdown was indeed successful: it is now rare for demonstrators to pelt state forces with stones, as they did regularly in the past. 60 Crisis Group interview, mid-level security official, Srinagar, 2025. But the change did not put an end to militancy in Kashmir, which appears to have adapted to the new environment. C. A New Breed of Insurgents? Over the decade leading up to 2019, militants were largely locals who openly used social media and relied on overground networks for logistics and recruitment. After New Delhi stepped up its counter-insurgency campaign in August 2019, militants not only altered their tactics, but they also went deep underground, becoming “lone wolves” who leave few physical or digital traces, making it much harder to pursue them. 61 Of late, militants have also avoided using intermediaries who can be monitored or technology that can be tracked. Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Jammu and Kashmir, Srinagar, November 2023-November 2025. Indian officials say many of the attacks that followed imposition of central rule were perpetrated by young people with no prior links to militancy – a profile they describe as the “hybrid militant”. 62 Some Indian officials claim that Pakistan-based militant groups are behind this tactical shift. “Hybrid militancy a ‘strategic move’ by Pakistan: J&K police chief”, Deccan Herald , 22 July 2022; “Shadow militants: Why a policeman’s killing has shaken a battle-hardened Kashmiri village”, Scroll.in , 16 August 2022. Officials allege that these recruits have often carried out a single attack, at the behest of Pakistani handlers, and then returned to their normal lives. 63 “Inside the shadowy, deadly world of Kashmir’s teenage hybrid militants”, Article 14 , 6 October 2022. A second change in militancy after August 2019 relates to its geographic spread. As New Delhi focused its campaign on the Kashmir valley, militants increasingly staged their attacks in the Jammu region, south of the valley across the Pir Panjal mountains. The first major ambush in Jammu took place in October 2021, when militants killed five soldiers, gunning down four more during the search operation that followed. 64 “New terror push in Jammu, Gujjar, Bakherwal alienation: Why the deaths of 5 soldiers underline the security challenge in Poonch”, The Indian Express , 5 May 2023. The militants’ rationale for extending their fight southward was likely twofold: a recalibration to escape the larger troop deployment and a wish to spare Kashmiri Muslims the state’s reprisals. 65 Crisis Group interviews, security officials and civil society figures, Jammu and Srinagar, December 2025. The magnitude of the challenge became clear as the encounters with state forces increased. Attacks in Jammu, which had been formally declared free of militancy in 2020, accounted for 40 per cent of all security personnel killed in Jammu and Kashmir between 2021 and 2024. 66 “Since 2021, Jammu accounts for 40% of killings of security personnel in J&K”, The Hindu , 17 July 2024. By 2025, a senior police officer said, the authorities were conducting an average of 120 anti-militancy operations per day in the region. 67 “120 anti-terror ops launched daily in Jammu to eliminate foreign terrorists: IGP”, Greater Kashmir , 21 October 2025. The resurgence of violence in Jammu after almost two decades of peace caught the Indian security establishment off guard. The resurgence of violence in Jammu after almost two decades of peace caught the Indian security establishment off guard. State forces had grown complacent amid the peace that had prevailed in the decade prior to 2019. Their numbers had also been depleted in 2020, when New Delhi transferred troops to Ladakh after the border clash with Chinese troops that April. 68 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Report N°334, Thin Ice in the Himalayas: Handling the India-China Border Dispute , 14 November 2023. Crucial intelligence networks also broke down following the declaration of central rule over the region. Time and again, the authorities found that their old informers were acting as double agents for the militants. By 2020, the Jammu and Kashmir security apparatus decided to stop relying on informers, notwithstanding the ill effects on their intelligence-gathering capabilities. 69 Many smugglers who had been acting as informers were also cast aside. Crisis Group interview, security official, Jammu, 2025. Later, New Delhi also lost the services of the Gujjars and Bakkarwals, two nomadic tribes who live at high altitudes and had long been the state’s eyes and ears along remote border stretches, particularly as regards early warning of infiltration from Pakistan. These tribes were disgruntled by Indian government actions in the region. When they proved disinclined to cooperate with the authorities, officers suspected them of aiding the militants and meted out punishments allegedly including extrajudicial killings, exacerbating their estrangement from the state. 70 Gujjars and Bakkarwals make up 12 per cent of the population in Jammu and Kashmir. Their discontent stems from the BJP’s decision to grant Scheduled Tribe status, which confers benefits such as quotas for government jobs, to another ethnic group in 2023, sowing fear among them that their own share of these benefits would be reduced. “A people without voice: Why are Gujjars in Jammu region feeling under siege?”, Scroll.in , 8 October 2017; “Gujjar-Bakarwal agitation: Why Kashmiri tribals are up in arms”, Frontline , 10 August 2023. On the crackdown, see “From Where the Orders Came: Army officers testify that two generals oversaw the torture and murder of civilians in Poonch”, The Caravan , 1 February 2025; “‘Extra-judicial’ killings can alienate Gujjars from security forces: Intel”, The Tribune , 28 July 2025. By 2023, militant attacks had become so regular in Jammu that the government was forced to revive a defunct militia known as the Village Defence Guards, arming and training hundreds of villagers across the region. 71 These militias were first formed in the mid-1990s, at the height of the Kashmiri insurgency, but the government disbanded them when militancy declined. “India revives civil militia after Hindu killings in Kashmir”, AP, 28 February 2023. On 9 June 2024, just hours after Prime Minister Modi was sworn in for a third consecutive term, militants assailed a bus carrying Hindu pilgrims, killing nine and injuring more than 30 in Jammu’s Reasi district. 72 “Terrorist attack at Reasi sets alarm bells ringing in India’s security establishment”, The Diplomat , 20 June 2024. The attack appeared to have been timed to contradict the government’s narrative of a peaceful region open for visitors. 73 Crisis Group noted in 2022 that tourists “could well become targets, particularly if the government continues to insist that robust tourism is a sign of normalcy”.
